chunks: Al-Saffar from Ibrahim ibn Hashim from Yahya ibn al-Mubarak from Abdullah ibn Jabala from Isḥaq ibn 'Ammar from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

I said to him: A man became ill and bought his own soul from Allah for one hundred thousand dirhams, [vowing that] if Allah healed him from his illness and he recovered, [the money would be for Him]. He said: 'O Isḥaq, to whom did you dedicate it?' I said: 'I am your ransom, [I dedicated it] to the Imam.' He said: 'Yes, it is for Allah, and whatever is for Allah, it is for the Imam.'
ai.seo_question: Who receives the money vowed to Allah for healing?
ai.summary: In this narration from Sahih al-Tusi, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies the destination of funds vowed to Allah, ruling that they belong to the Imam, thereby establishing the Imam's authority over religious dedications. This highlights the Shia concept of the Imam as the rightful recipient of specific divine gifts and vows, linking spiritual devotion with temporal leadership. The dialogue underscores the precision required in vow-making and the Imam's role in managing communal religious resources.
